newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: No winner in failed Philippine bank merger talks.
newsitem.headline: No winner in failed Philippine bank merger talks.

text.p: AsianBank Corp and PDCP Bank have both lost a timely opportunity to boost their presence in the crowded Philippine banking industry after calling off their merger plan, analysts said on Tuesday.

"They're both losers here. They're both small banks and the best thing they should have done was to merge. The name of the game right now is size," Audi Pantillano, an analyst at Angping Securities, said.

A merger would have increased their combined capital to 6.6 billion pesos ($250.3 million) and branch network to 140, making the merged bank the 15th largest in a field of over 50 commercial banks in the country.
There might be other partners for both banks, but the chances of them surviving with their identities intact are remote, Pantillano said.
Under their original plan, PDCP initially would have retained its status as a publicly listed company, though AsianBank would have eventually taken over the operations.
A thrift bank subsidiary would then be created to take on the target clientele of PDCP.
However, AsianBank and PDCP Bank jointly announced late Monday that they would not proceed with the merger due to disagreements over their respective valuations.
The talks collapsed after two months of intense negotiations, PDCP executive vice president Michael Goco said.

The majority owners of both banks -- Metro Pacific Corp for PDCP Bank, and A Soriano Corp and Bacnotan Consolidated Industries for AsianBank -- announced their intention to merge in November last year, but actual negotiations started only after the two banks completed their 1996 audited financial reports in March.
Both banks said they would pursue talks with other prospective partners to be able to join the big league.
Rachel Evangelista, a banking analyst at All AsiaCapital and Trust Corp, said the failed merger has delayed their chance to outgun the competition early in the game.
The banking system is expected to grow in step with the booming domestic economy.

"They've lost that opportunity," she said. She added that she had already downgraded her recommendation on PDCP from a speculative buy to a hold as early as April after talk that the merger negotiations were in trouble.
On the stock market, PDCP's share price slumped 18 percent to 20.50 pesos following the news. AsianBank is not listed.
Evangelista said PDCP also had to sort out its 1996 merger with First Bank. "They're still trying to work out the synergy."
"It's not going to be the end of the world for both of us. We have to go on and continue what we are doing. It will just delay our plans a bit," PDCP's Goco said.
BNP Prime East analyst Marco Lucena said the failed talks would not affect future merger talks in the industry.
Analysts expect more merger talks especially among medium-sized banks to strengthen their position in the booming banking sector. ($1 = 26.37 pesos)
